title: The wheel of offering
hookLine: rain, grain, a meal, and the Gita calls anyone who breaks the circle a thief
carry: yajna: offer first, then eat what's given back
tomorrow: bhakti: the universe in a toddler's mouth

cards: Last night's dinner had a long history. A store, sure. Before that, a truck, a farm, a field.
Before that, seed and soil and sun, and rain, a lot of rain, falling on land nobody at the table has seen. Many people's work, and a sky nobody at the table arranged.
And it can all vanish in ten minutes, in front of a phone. The Gita's third chapter has a strong word for someone who takes all that and gives nothing back. Thief.

teach.b: Krishna has just told Arjuna he can't stop acting. Now he explains how action stops binding you. Everything done as yajna, he says, doesn't bind; everything else ties the world in knots.
Yajna is the old word for the Vedic fire offering: grain and butter poured into the flames, given to the gods. Then Krishna tells a creation story.

In the beginning, the creator made beings together with offering, and said: by this, may you flourish. Nourish the gods with it, and they will nourish you, and caring for each other, you'll reach the highest good.

teach.h: WHO TAKES AND NEVER GIVES IS A THIEF.
teach.b: Whoever enjoys the gifts without giving anything back is simply a thief. The good, who eat what's left after the offering, are freed; those who cook only for themselves eat wrongdoing.
That is the root of what Hindu families do every day: food is offered to God first, then eaten as prasad, what is left after the offering. Then comes the wheel. Beings come from food.
Food from rain. Rain from offering. Offering from action.
It's a circle, and whoever doesn't help turn it, Krishna says, lives in vain. And if you've never lit a sacred fire?

teach.h: SEND SOMETHING BACK INTO THE CIRCLE.
teach.b: The Gita's next chapter names many kinds of yajna, and some Hindu teachers read it wider still: any action done as a gift back into the circle. Cooking for your family. Paying fairly.
Planting something. Teaching a kid to read.
The Gita isn't saying don't enjoy. It's saying enjoy as someone who knows where things come from, and send something back. That's what makes action free instead of binding.
You're no longer grabbing. You're turning the wheel.

how: Many Hindus offer food to God before eating and receive it back as prasad, and some recite a Gita verse before meals; the idea of yajna as any action offered back into the world is common in modern Hindu teaching.

o: action, offered back into the circle of giving
a punishment for taking more than your share
fate that decides how your harvest turns out

games.q: the wheel of chapter three — tap the pairs.

s: the Gita says enjoying anything binds you
it says action done as offering doesn't bind; the problem is taking without giving back.
in chapter three, rain comes from offering
food from rain, rain from offering, offering from action: the wheel.
the Gita calls those who cook only for themselves good people
it says the good eat what's left after the offering.

games.q: you've enjoyed a good harvest, a good meal, a good year. according to Krishna in chapter three, what's the next step?
o: keep it all: you earned it.
give something back into the circle.
stop eating to avoid binding karma.
games.why: whoever enjoys the gifts without giving back is a thief. action as offering turns the wheel and doesn't bind.

practice: Bring to mind something you'll eat or use today, and follow it back slowly: the hands that packed it, the truck and the driver, the field, the farmer, the rain.
Breathe in and receive all of it; breathe out and ask what small thing you could send back into the circle. If you pray, you can offer your next meal before eating it, as some Hindus do.

wordCard.voice: Karma. Action. In the Gita's third chapter, action done as offering, yajna, turns the great wheel instead of tying knots.

orig.note: Sanskrit: sacrifice, offering; the Vedic fire rite, from yaj, to worship or offer.

carryVoice: Keep this: yajna. Offer first, then eat what's given back. Every meal started as rain. Day three hundred five, done.

sources.ref: Bhagavad Gita 3.10–3.16 (creation with offering; the thief; the remains of offering; the wheel)
